claims.text: Introducing controlled amounts of oxygen or nitrogen into the high-entropy alloy can reduce post-exposure toughness degradation.
Interstitial oxygen or nitrogen initially contributes to solid-solution strengthening in a high-entropy alloy.
Interstitial additions reduce depletion of solute interstitials from the alloy matrix during heating.
Interstitial additions inhibit deleterious phase segregation during thermal exposure.
Phase segregation is a relevant structural mediator during thermal exposure of refractory high-entropy alloys.
Maintaining interstitial solid-solution strengthening and suppressing phase segregation will maintain toughness after heating.
The treated alloy will exhibit less post-exposure toughness degradation than an otherwise untreated alloy.
The proposed intervention is applicable throughout a heating range of 500°C to 800°C.
The proposed intervention is applicable for exposure durations of up to 100 hours.
The hypothesis applies under tensile or compressive loading.
Grain size and precipitates may affect the alloy's toughness response to interstitial additions and heating.
The optimal amount and type of interstitial addition are not established.
A dose-series experiment including interstitial-treated samples and an untreated baseline can test the predicted toughness retention.
Charpy impact or fracture-toughness testing can measure the post-exposure toughness response.
Electron microscopy can test whether interstitial treatment changes phase segregation after exposure.
Failure to obtain a significant reduction in toughness degradation, or failure to observe the proposed microstructural differences, would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The proposed mechanism says oxygen or nitrogen inhibits phase segregation and reduces interstitial depletion, whereas record node::10.1126/sciadv.adj1511 reports that trace oxygen and nitrogen promote phase segregation during aging, leading to depletion of interstitials from the matrix and progressive softening.
